passage: I'm Avni, Vinita's flatmate. Last year Vinita's father had a heart attack at fifty-two. After he recovered, she did something I didn't expect. She sat with him and wrote down the family's health history: heart problems on his side, diabetes on her mother's. Then she booked a basic check-up for herself at twenty-five. I thought it was a bit much. She said, "The doctor can tell me what's worth tracking, and I'd rather know early." She came back with a small notebook where she writes her results and questions for the doctor. She also started walking to work. She isn't anxious about it, just steady. Last month I asked her to help me make my own list.

qa.q: What health problem runs on Vinita's father's side?
qa.a: Heart problems run on his side.

qa.q: What does Vinita's 'I'd rather know early' reveal about her thinking?
qa.a: It shows she feels calm and determined to understand her risks early, while there's still time to act.

qa.q: What preventive steps did Vinita take?
qa.a: She wrote down the family health history, booked a check-up, kept a notebook of results and started walking to work.

qa.q: How did Avni's view of Vinita's check-up change?
qa.a: At first Avni thought it was too much, but later asked for help making her own list.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a young woman track family health risk and seek preventive care early.

passage:
Week one: Pankaj, twenty-four, laughed when his sister Aadhya told him to get a check-up. "I play football. I'm fine."

Week three: At the family lunch, their uncle spoke about his kidney problem, found late. Aadhya caught Pankaj's eye across the table. He looked away, uncomfortable.

Week six: Pankaj went to the clinic near his office. The doctor asked about family history, which he didn't know. He called his mother from the waiting room. The doctor explained which tests made sense for him and said to come back if anything worried him. The results were mostly fine; one number was worth watching. Pankaj started keeping his reports in a folder. He texted Aadhya: 'Okay. You were right. Don't gloat.'

qa.q: Where did Pankaj go for his check-up?
qa.a: He went to the clinic near his office.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj look away when Aadhya caught his eye?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable, realising his uncle's late-found illness made her point hard to ignore.

qa.q: What helped Pankaj move from dismissing check-ups to getting one?
qa.a: Hearing about his uncle's illness made the risk feel real, and his sister's steady nudging kept him thinking.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel reading Pankaj's text?
qa.a: She might feel relieved and quietly pleased that he took care of himself. 😊

grounding: Shows a young man over several weeks moving from dismissing check-ups to seeking preventive care.

passage: Farida beta, sit with your Dilnaz-khala a minute. When I was your age, I never went to a doctor unless I was sick. My mother had diabetes, but I thought, that's her, not me. I felt tired for years and blamed my job. At thirty, I fainted at a wedding. Only then did I find out my sugar had been high for a long time. The doctor said if I'd known earlier, it might have been easier to manage. I'm fine now, but I have to be very careful. So, you know your grandmother's history, your mother's too. Talk to your doctor about what to check. Not because you're ill. Because you're not, and you want to stay that way.

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz faint?
qa.a: She fainted at a wedding.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz ignore her tiredness for years?
qa.a: She thought her mother's diabetes had nothing to do with her and blamed her job instead.

qa.q: What advice does Dilnaz give Farida?
qa.a: Know the family history and talk to a doctor about what to check, even when feeling well.

qa.q: How might Farida see her aunt's story?
qa.a: It may make the family risk feel real to her, since it happened to someone she knows. 🙏

grounding: Shows an elder urging a young relative to be aware of family health risk and seek preventive care.

passage:
The free checkup camp in the office lobby closed at noon, and Shalini's client call was at 11:30.
She stood in the queue anyway, laptop bag cutting into her shoulder, rereading a text from her sister Kavitha: "Did you go? Amma's sugar was high again 😔"
Both their grandmothers had diabetes. Amma found out only after years of tiredness she'd blamed on work. Shalini had promised herself she wouldn't wait for a symptom.
At 11:20 she was still six people back. She asked the nurse if she could give the blood sample now and fill the form later. The nurse nodded.
She joined the call from a plastic chair with a cotton ball taped to her arm. That evening she made a note on her phone: family history, results date, ask the doctor when to come back. Then she texted Kavitha: "Done. Your turn 🙂"

qa.q: What time was Shalini's client call?
qa.a: The call was at 11:30, and the camp closed at noon.

qa.q: Why was Shalini determined to get checked despite the clash?
qa.a: She had seen Amma find out about her diabetes only after years of ignored tiredness, and she didn't want to wait for symptoms herself.

qa.q: What small step helped Shalini fit the checkup in?
qa.a: She asked the nurse if she could give the sample first and fill the form later, which saved both her place and her call.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel reading 'Done. Your turn'?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved about Shalini and gently nudged to look after her own health too 😊

grounding: Shows a young woman keeping track of family health risk and making time for a preventive checkup despite a work clash.

passage:
The pharmacy at the corner of Hemant's colony had a blood-pressure machine by the door, and Omkar dared him to try it while they waited for cough syrup.
Hemant laughed, then didn't. His father and his uncle both took heart tablets now, and at the last family wedding the aunties had talked about it the way people discuss the weather.
The reading came out higher than the chart on the wall suggested. The pharmacist said one machine reading didn't mean much, but that it was worth seeing a doctor.
That night Hemant phoned his mother and asked, a little awkwardly, for everyone's health conditions on both sides of the family. She sounded surprised, then pleased. He wrote them in a notebook and booked a clinic appointment for Saturday.
Omkar, watching from the sofa, quietly booked one too.

qa.q: Who dared Hemant to use the machine?
qa.a: Omkar, while they were waiting for cough syrup.

qa.q: What does Hemant's laugh fading suggest about his thoughts?
qa.a: The joke suddenly felt serious because he remembered his father and uncle both take heart tablets, and he felt a flicker of worry.

qa.q: What did the pharmacist's response get right?
qa.a: It didn't alarm Hemant or claim to know what was wrong; it said one reading meant little but pointed him to a doctor.

qa.q: Why might Hemant's mother sound pleased by his call?
qa.a: She may be glad her son is taking the family's health history seriously and asking before any problem shows up.

grounding: Shows a young man starting to track family health risk and booking preventive care after a small warning sign.
